prompt: Every exchange is a request and a response
body: HTTP is a conversation of structured text. A client (your browser, curl, an app) sends a request: a method and URL on the first line, then headers like Host and Accept, then an optional body. The server answers with a response: a status line like HTTP/2 200, then its own headers, then usually a body. Nothing magical happens in between: one process wrote bytes down a socket and another read them. When an API misbehaves, you debug it by reading those bytes, which is what tools like curl -v expose.

hints.text: Both messages have the same three-part shape: start line, headers, body.

check.prompt: In the response HTTP/2 200, what does the 200 describe?
check.answer: The outcome of handling the request: success

prompt: Your terminal runs curl. In HTTP terms, what is curl?

options.text: A protocol between client and server

hints.text: Who speaks first in the exchange?

explanation: curl is an HTTP client: it sends requests and prints responses. HTTP is the protocol; curl is a program.

prompt: Which parts does an HTTP request always contain?

options.text: A method, a URL, and a JSON body
A status code and a body

hints.text: The mandatory first line names an action and a target.

explanation: Method and URL are required. Bodies are optional, and status codes belong to responses.

prompt: Teach it back: describe one full request-response exchange, naming the parts of each message.
modelAnswer: The client sends a request: method and URL on the first line, headers like Host and Accept, optional body. The server replies: a status line such as HTTP/2 200, headers like Content-Type, and a body. Example: curl requests GET https://example.com and receives 200 with HTML.

hints.text: Three parts per message, plus one concrete example.

prompt: Lab: your first request

hints.text: Look for the blank line that separates headers from the body.

prompt: Reading a URL
body: A URL names a resource. It reads in order: scheme://host/path?query. The scheme (https) says how to talk, the host (api.github.com) says which server, the path (/repos/michael-borck/cairn) says which resource on that server, and the query string (?page=2&per_page=50) carries parameters as key=value pairs joined by &. The path identifies; the query adjusts. Anything after the ? is not part of the resource's address, which is also why query strings are the wrong place for secrets.

hints.text: Find the ? first: it splits the address from the parameters.

check.answer: A query parameter: key q with value cairn

prompt: In https://api.github.com/repos/michael-borck/cairn?per_page=5, what is api.github.com?

options.text: The host that will answer the request

hints.text: It sits between the // and the first single /.

explanation: api.github.com is the host. The path starts after it, and per_page=5 is a query parameter.

prompt: Which URL asks page 2 with 50 results per page?

hints.text: Parameters live after a ? and join with &.

explanation: Query parameters come after the path: ?key=value&key=value.

prompt: Lab: send query parameters

hints.text: Quote the URL: unquoted & means run-in-background to the shell.

prompt: Methods and what they promise
body: The method says what you intend to do. GET reads without changing anything. POST creates something new; calling it twice usually creates two things. PUT replaces a resource's whole representation with what you send. PATCH changes only the fields you send. DELETE removes. The useful property here is idempotence: an operation is idempotent if calling it once or five times ends in the same state. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. This is why retrying a failed POST can double-charge a card, and why APIs use idempotency keys to make retries safe.

hints.text: Ask of each method: if the network drops and I send it again, is the world still consistent?

check.prompt: A payment POST times out. Why is blind retrying dangerous?
check.answer: POST is not idempotent; the first attempt may have succeeded, so a retry could charge twice

prompt: Which method is NOT idempotent?

hints.text: Which method can create a new thing every time it runs?

explanation: Repeated POSTs can create duplicates. GET, PUT, and DELETE converge to the same state.

prompt: You want to change just the email field of a user record. Which request fits?

hints.text: PUT replaces the whole representation; you only have one field.

explanation: PATCH sends a partial change. PUT with a one-field body implies the other fields are gone.

prompt: Walk through: rename a widget from wren to finch without losing its colour field.

steps.title: Choose the method
steps.body: You have one field to change. PATCH /widgets/12 with {"name": "finch"} keeps colour untouched.

steps.title: Why not PUT
steps.body: PUT /widgets/12 with {"name": "finch"} would declare the whole resource is now just that; colour would be gone.

checkpoint.prompt: Which method changes one field without touching the rest?

hints.text: Whole replacement versus partial change.

scaffolds.prompt: The request only carries the name field. Which method promises to leave colour alone?

hints.text: P stands for partial.

scaffolds.prompt: What does PUT with a partial body imply about the missing fields?
scaffolds.answer: That they no longer exist; PUT replaces the whole representation

prompt: Lab: echo a POST and a PUT

hints.text: Escape the inner quotes of the JSON body carefully, or use single quotes outside.

prompt: Status codes come in families
body: The first digit tells you the family. 2xx succeeded (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content). 3xx redirected (301 moved for good, 302 moved for now); the answer lives in the Location header. 4xx means the client must change something: 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated (who are you?), 403 unauthorised (I know you, and no), 404 not found, 429 too many requests. 5xx means the server tripped: 500 generic error, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable. Debug rule: 4xx is your bug, 5xx is theirs.

hints.text: Read only the first digit first, then learn four or six specific codes.

check.prompt: You call an API without credentials and get 401. What must you change?
check.answer: Send credentials, for example an Authorization header

prompt: What does a 302 response tell the client to do?

options.text: Look at the Location header and go there next

hints.text: 3xx is not an error family.

explanation: 302 is a redirect: the response's Location header names the next address to try.

prompt: curl prints HTTP/2 301 for an old URL you still have bookmarked. What happened?

options.text: The resource moved permanently; a Location header names the new address
The server crashed with an internal error
Your request had a syntax error

hints.text: 301 is the permanent half of the 3xx family.

explanation: 301 Moved Permanently: update the bookmark. curl -L follows it automatically.

prompt: An API answers 401. What does the server not know?

options.text: Who you are; you sent no valid credentials
Who you are, and it refuses your access

hints.text: 401 asks a question; 403 answers no.

explanation: 401 Unauthenticated: send credentials. 403 Forbidden: identity accepted, access denied.

prompt: Lab: collect status codes

hints.text: The -w format string prints only the code, which makes comparing easy.

prompt: Headers describe the message
body: Headers are key: value pairs that carry metadata. The ones to know first: Content-Type describes the body you are sending (application/json is the API default); Accept says what you will take back, which is content negotiation; Authorization carries credentials such as Bearer tokens; Cache-Control and ETag manage caching so clients can reuse unmodified resources. Content-Type belongs to requests that have a body; a bodyless GET has nothing to describe. When a server answers with a surprising format, check whether you negotiated it with Accept.

hints.text: One header describes what you send, another what you want back.

check.prompt: Which header would you set to ask a server for JSON?

prompt: You POST a JSON body. Which header must accompany it?

hints.text: You are describing the body you are sending.

explanation: Content-Type declares the body you send. Accept negotiates the response format.

prompt: A bodyless GET carries Content-Type: application/json. What does that accomplish?

options.text: Nothing useful; a GET has no body to describe, and the header you wanted is Accept
It forces the server to answer in JSON

hints.text: Content describes the body you send; a GET sends none.

explanation: Content-Type on a bodyless GET is a no-op. To ask for JSON back, send Accept: application/json.

prompt: Lab: negotiate a content type

hints.text: Change only the Accept header between the two calls.

prompt: Reading JSON
body: JSON is a text format with exactly six kinds of value: objects ({}), arrays ([]), strings, numbers, true/false, and null. Objects map keys to values with double-quoted keys; arrays are ordered lists. Nesting is how APIs express structure: a repository object can contain an owner object, which contains a login string, reached as repo.owner.login. JSON is stricter than JavaScript object literals: double quotes only, no trailing commas, no comments. Reading a big response is easier if you pull one field out instead of scanning the wall of text.

hints.text: Curly braces are lookups by name; square brackets are ordered lists.

check.prompt: In {"owner": {"login": "michael-borck"}}, how do you reach the login value?
check.answer: owner.login, an object nested inside another object

prompt: Which of these is valid JSON?

hints.text: JSON accepts only one kind of quote and hates trailing commas.

explanation: Double quotes are required and trailing commas are illegal; both other candidates came from JavaScript habits.

prompt: Given {"license": {"spdx_id": "MIT"}, "stargazers_count": 42}, which expression reads the licence id?

hints.text: spdx_id lives inside the license object; walk down through it.

explanation: license is an object, so you look up spdx_id inside it: license.spdx_id.

prompt: Lab: pull one field from JSON

hints.text: Pipe curl's output into python3 and load it with json.load(sys.stdin).

prompt: API keys and bearer tokens
body: APIs need to know who is calling. The common patterns: an API key, a long string that identifies you, sent in a header like X-API-Key; and bearer tokens, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>, which is how OAuth 2 flows hand out access. Both are secrets. They belong in environment variables or a credential store, never in source code, and never in URLs, which end up in server logs, browser history, and proxies. Base64 encoding a secret is not protection: encoding is reversible by anyone. If a key leaks, revoke it and issue a new one; rotation is routine, not an emergency measure to avoid.

hints.text: Ask of any secret: where does this string travel, and who can copy it on the way?

check.prompt: Why is Authorization: Bearer x better than ?token=x in the URL?
check.answer: Headers are not logged the way URLs are; URLs get stored in logs, history, and proxies

prompt: Where should your API token live while you develop?

options.text: In an environment variable or system credential store
In a config file committed to the repo, base64-encoded for safety
In the request URL so the request is self-contained

hints.text: Two traps here: encoding is not hiding, and URLs leak.

explanation: Env vars and credential stores keep secrets out of code and logs. Base64 decodes trivially, and URLs get logged everywhere.

prompt: You accidentally pushed a real token to a public repo. What is the right response?

options.text: Delete the commit; if the file is gone it is safe
Revoke the token immediately, then clean the history
Nothing; the repo is new and nobody saw it

hints.text: Assume anything ever public is already copied by crawlers.

explanation: Bots scan public repos within minutes. Revocation kills the leaked credential regardless of who holds a copy; history cleanup is second.

prompt: Teach it back: how is a bearer token sent, which two places must never hold a secret, and what do you do when one leaks?
modelAnswer: Sent in the Authorization header as Bearer <token>. Secrets never live in source control or in URLs, which are logged. On leak: revoke immediately and issue a replacement, then scrub the history.

hints.text: Three parts: the header, the two forbidden places, the leak procedure.

prompt: Lab: send a bearer token

hints.text: Compare only the status code of the two calls.

prompt: REST is nouns plus methods
body: A well-designed API names resources as nouns and lets the method carry the verb: GET /users lists, POST /users creates, GET /users/7 reads one, PATCH /users/7 edits, DELETE /users/7 removes. Collections are plural; members hang off them. Filtering, sorting, and pagination belong in query parameters, not in new paths: /items?page=2&per_page=50&sort=created. When an endpoint grows verbs like /getUser or /deleteItem, that is RPC thinking wearing a REST URL, and it usually means the method semantics are being duplicated in the path.

hints.text: Read a URL and ask: is this a thing, or an instruction?

check.prompt: Which URL reads page 3 of the items collection?

prompt: Which design reads one item and then deletes it, REST-style?

hints.text: The method is the verb; the URL is only the noun.

explanation: REST lets DELETE carry the removal. Verb-named paths duplicate what methods already say.

prompt: Where does a REST API usually put pagination parameters?

options.text: In new paths for each page: /items/page/2
In the request body of a GET

hints.text: Pagination adjusts a listing rather than naming a new resource.

explanation: Query parameters adjust a collection. Page-shaped paths multiply endpoints for the same resource.

prompt: Reflect: find one public API you use (GitHub, a weather service, anything) and write down two of its URLs. Are they nouns? Do the query parameters adjust listings?
prompts: Which API did you pick, and what are its resource URLs?
Do the paths read as nouns with methods doing the verbs?
Where does that API put pagination and filtering?

hints.text: The GitHub REST API docs are a good specimen if you have none in mind.

prompt: Errors, timeouts, and polite retries
body: Three failure modes matter. A 4xx tells you your request was wrong; do not retry it unchanged. A 429 says slow down; honour the Retry-After header if present. A 5xx or a network timeout means the far end struggled; retrying can help, but wait between attempts and grow the wait each time (exponential backoff, for example 1s, 2s, 4s). Two cautions. First, a 200 status does not guarantee success: some APIs wrap business errors in a 200 body, so read both signals. Second, a timeout does not mean the server stopped: it may still be processing, which is why POST retries need idempotency keys.

hints.text: Classify first: my bug, their bug, or too fast?

check.prompt: You get 429 with Retry-After: 30. What do you do?
check.answer: Wait 30 seconds, then retry; do not hammer the endpoint

prompt: A batch job hits 429 responses. Which retry behaviour is correct?

options.text: Retry instantly in a tight loop until it succeeds
Wait, growing the wait each attempt, and honour Retry-After
Give up permanently on the first 429

hints.text: The server is telling you a rate; read what it says and slow down.

explanation: Exponential backoff with Retry-After respected is the polite and effective pattern.

prompt: A payment POST times out after 30s. Why is a plain retry dangerous?

options.text: The first request may still have succeeded, so the retry could pay twice
Timeouts are always caused by your own network, so retrying never helps

hints.text: Your client gave up; nobody told the server to stop.

explanation: The server may have completed the charge after your client gave up. Idempotency keys exist precisely for this.

prompt: An API answers 200 OK but the body is {"error": "insufficient_funds"}. What happened?

options.text: The transport succeeded; the business operation failed. Your code must read the body
Nothing; 200 means the payment went through
The server is broken and must be reported to its operator

hints.text: Status code and body are two separate signals.

explanation: Some APIs reserve HTTP errors for transport problems and put business outcomes in the body. Trusting the code alone misses the failure.

prompt: Reading the wire with curl -v
body: curl -v prints the whole conversation. Lines starting with > are what your client sent; lines starting with < are what the server returned; * lines are curl's own commentary about connections and TLS. With redirects and -L, you get one status line per hop, so you can watch a 301 turn into a 200. When an API behaves differently in your code than in the docs, run the same request with curl -v before blaming either side: the exchange shows exactly which headers went out and what came back.

hints.text: Point one way: > is yours, < is theirs.

check.prompt: In curl -v output, which character marks response headers?
check.answer: <, the less-than sign, marks what came back from the server

prompt: In curl -v output, what does a line beginning with > contain?

options.text: Something your client sent to the server

hints.text: The arrow points away from you on the way out.

explanation: > marks request material, < marks response material, * marks curl's own notes.

prompt: curl -vL on a redirecting URL shows two status lines: 302 then 200. What does that prove?

options.text: The client followed the Location header and made a second request
The server sent the final body twice
The connection was retried after a timeout

hints.text: One request per status line.

explanation: -L follows redirects, so each hop gets its own exchange in the log.

prompt: Lab: read the whole exchange

hints.text: Count the status lines to count the hops.
